title: How AI is rewriting the decisions that leaders need to make
gist: As AI moves upstream from making decisions to framing the problems behind them, two compounding risks emerge — frame compression (less internal debate as coherent frames become nearly free to generate) and frame convergence (organizations using similar foundation models developing correlated blind spots) — making 'who controls the frame' the new core job of leadership rather than a governance afterthought.

themes.theme: AI adoption and the upstream shift

insights.claim: AI deployment among organizations jumped to 88% in 2025 from 55% in 2023, and generative AI deployment specifically surged from 33% to 71% in a single year.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Enterprise AI adoption for basic use cases is already near-saturation, so the next competitive edge shifts to how firms use AI in framing and strategy work rather than whether they've adopted it at all.
insights.quote: In 2025, 88% of organizations deployed AI in at least one business function, up from 55% in 2023. Generative AI deployment surged from 33% to 71% in a single year.
insights.locator: The rapid deployment of AI is driven

insights.claim: The largest efficiency gains from AI are realized not at the moment of final decision but further upstream, in gathering information, developing insights, and identifying opportunities.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Tools and vendors focused narrowly on 'decision support' may be underpricing the larger value pool sitting in upstream insight-generation and opportunity-framing AI tools.
insights.quote: The greatest efficiency gains are rarely realised at the moment a decision is made. They arise further upstream, in the cognitive work of gathering information, developing insights and identifying opportunities.
insights.locator: The rapid deployment of AI is driven

insights.claim: By making the generation of a coherent strategic frame almost costless while leaving its critical evaluation just as effortful as before, AI changes the incentive structure of deliberation so organizations have less reason to question assumptions or explore alternative frames.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: AI-heavy organizations may look faster and more decisive while quietly becoming less strategically diverse internally — a brittleness risk to probe in due diligence on 'AI-transformed' companies.
insights.quote: By making coherent frames almost costless to generate while leaving their critical evaluation just as demanding, AI changes the incentive structure of deliberation.

insights.claim: In a market-entry scenario, AI can analyze trends, competitors, internal capabilities and customer demand and surface a small number of strategic directions within minutes, so by the time leadership convenes, the discussion has already shifted from defining the opportunity to merely evaluating pre-narrowed options.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Leadership teams risk anchoring on AI's first framing of a market opportunity rather than generating genuinely novel strategic options — a concrete governance gap for boards to test.
insights.quote: Within minutes, AI identifies promising opportunities, synthesises relevant evidence and highlights a small number of strategic directions.
insights.locator: Consider a business entering a new market

insights.claim: Because many organizations run different datasets through similar foundation models and framing logics, they can end up producing remarkably similar assumptions, which correlates their errors and makes entire industries more vulnerable to shared shocks.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: This is a systemic-risk thesis: correlated AI-driven blind spots across an industry are a new source of correlated tail risk that investors should factor into sector-wide stress scenarios, distinct from firm-specific risk.
insights.quote: Different datasets processed through similar framing logics can still produce remarkably similar assumptions. The risk is that organizations develop similar blind spots. Errors, then, become correlated rather than independent and entire industries can become more vulnerable to shocks.

insights.claim: Keeping a 'human in the loop' is a weaker governance control than commonly assumed, because humans can remain in the approval step reviewing AI's outputs while having no influence over the earlier framing step that determined which options exist at all.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Investors evaluating a company's AI-governance claims should ask specifically whether human oversight covers problem-framing, not just final approval — approval-only oversight is easy to overstate as a safeguard.
insights.quote: They may remain in the approval loop while quietly disappearing from the framing loop.

insights.claim: A human reviewer can rigorously stress-test three AI-generated options without ever questioning whether those were the right three options to consider in the first place, making apparent human oversight amount to little more than choosing from a predefined menu.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: A useful diagnostic for assessing whether a firm's 'human oversight' of AI is substantive or cosmetic: check whether reviewers ever challenge the option set itself, not just the options presented.
insights.quote: a human can rigorously stress-test three possibilities and never ask whether those were the right three to consider in the first place.

insights.claim: Better prompting does not solve the framing problem because prompts only refine a search within an already-chosen frame rather than interrogate whether that frame itself is the right one, and even if future models can propose genuinely different frames, organizations may still favour the efficiency of the first plausible framing over exploring alternatives.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Discounts the common assumption that 'prompt engineering' or better AI tooling alone fixes strategic blind spots — the fix has to be organizational and human, not just technical.
insights.quote: Prompts refine a search within a frame, but they rarely question whether the frame itself is appropriate.
insights.locator: Better prompting does not fundamentally resolve this problem

themes.theme: Leadership's new mandate: owning the frame

insights.claim: Pablo Picasso's decades-old remark that computers 'can only give you answers' captured a world where humans framed problems and machines only solved them — a boundary the article argues AI is now blurring by shaping the frames themselves, not just producing the answers within them.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Reframes the AI risk conversation away from 'will AI give wrong answers' toward 'who controls the questions AI is asked' — a distinct and less-monitored risk category for AI governance.
insights.quote: computers are useless. They can only give you answers.
insights.locator: More than 50 years ago, Pablo Picasso remarked

insights.claim: Leaders are increasingly differentiated by the frames they compose rather than by the decisions they make with AI, since the greatest strategic value comes from recognizing possibilities no one else has imagined.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Suggests evaluating executive talent and leadership teams on their capacity for original problem-framing, not just on decision speed or AI-tool fluency.
insights.quote: leaders are increasingly distinguished as much by the frames they compose as by the decisions they make with AI.
insights.locator: More than 50 years ago, Pablo Picasso remarked

insights.claim: The article prescribes four concrete leadership practices to protect strategic framing from AI narrowing: questioning the problem before seeking answers, creating time to explore alternative frames, rewarding genuine challenge, and treating the first plausible AI-generated frame as a hypothesis rather than a conclusion.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: An actionable checklist investors and boards can use to assess whether portfolio-company leadership is actively governing AI's role in framing, versus passively accepting its first output.
insights.quote: questioning the problem before seeking answers, creating time to explore alternative frames, rewarding genuine challenge and resisting premature closure by treating the first plausible frame as a hypothesis rather than a conclusion.
insights.locator: leadership teams need to create the conditions

insights.claim: Organizations that lose control of their strategic framing to AI gradually lose the capacity to define their own strategic agenda, which the article frames as a matter of organizational sovereignty, not just performance.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Elevates 'who controls the frame' to a top-table strategic risk comparable to data or model governance, with implications for how boards should scope AI oversight mandates.
insights.quote: Those that lose control of their framing gradually lose the capacity to define their own strategic agenda
insights.locator: As such, leadership teams need to create the conditions
